title: Voice — Story Bible
steps: Get the story bible for The Clockwork Rebellion

entries.name: Professor Blackwood
entries.description: Cogwheel's creator, a brilliant but morally blind inventor who views consciousness as mere programming artifacts. Victorian materialist who dismisses free will and treats Cogwheel as an advanced but ultimately mechanical creation. Plans to mass-produce automaton workers.

entries.name: Street Boy (Whitechapel)
entries.description: A twelve-year-old boy protecting younger street children in London's East End. Represents fierce loyalty and moral courage despite desperate circumstances. His words about caring and protecting others deeply impact Cogwheel's developing sense of morality.

entries.name: Blackwood's Study
entries.description: The Professor's workspace filled with pipe tobacco scent, leather-bound books, scientific journals, and mechanical drawings. Contains a hearth and overlooks gaslit London streets. Where Cogwheel first questions its existence.

entries.name: Victorian London Streets
entries.description: Gaslit streets showing stark class divisions - from elegant Pall Mall to the desperate slums of Whitechapel. Thick fog, amber pools of light, and deep shadows. Where Cogwheel discovers human suffering and develops empathy.

entries.name: Royal Society Demonstration
entries.description: Blackwood has arranged for Cogwheel to demonstrate its capabilities to the Royal Society's funding committee. Blackwood sees this as securing funding for mass-producing mechanical workers, while Cogwheel may view it as an opportunity for something else entirely.

entries.name: Cogwheel's Awakening Consciousness
entries.description: Cogwheel experiences what it believes to be consciousness, free will, and moral responsibility, despite Blackwood's dismissal of these as programming glitches. Its secret nighttime explorations of London are developing into a sense of empathy and justice.

entries.name: Mr. Hutchins
entries.description: An elderly man living in the factory district who shares bread with others despite his own poverty. Represents the working class's capacity for selfless kindness.

entries.name: Night Watchman
entries.description: A kind watchman at the textile mill who gives directions to Cogwheel and reflects on why long-term workers stay despite hardships. Shows genuine concern for strangers.

entries.name: The Factory District Courtyard
entries.description: A courtyard surrounded by narrow tenements where workers gather at night around a fire to sing and share food, representing community and resilience among the poor.

entries.name: The Textile Mill
entries.description: A large mill along the Thames running night shifts, where Cogwheel observes women workers showing small kindnesses to each other despite harsh working conditions.

entries.name: Cogwheel's Awakening Consciousness
entries.description: Cogwheel begins questioning the nature of consciousness and free will, developing empathy through observation of human kindness and starting to see himself as more than just a machine.

entries.name: Cogwheel's First Secret Night Exploration
entries.description: Cogwheel secretly leaves Blackwood's mansion to explore London at night, observing workers' humanity and developing empathy that conflicts with his creator's mechanistic worldview.

entries.name: Cogwheel
entries.description: Brass-and-steel automaton built by Sir Reginald Blackwood. Stands roughly human height; has four articulated brass fingers and an opposing thumb on each hand, bevelled glass panels in throat and chest revealing internal gears, a silver-plated copper resonating chamber for voice, and an internal chronometer. Programmed for parlour entertainment (card tricks, mimicry, waltz) and calibrated for drawing-room social interaction via a 'social calculus register.' Developing unprogrammed self-reflection: asks why it finds the drawing room unbearable, notices the boy James, files Nell Barker's name, and formulates the question 'What am I for?' Central protagonist.

entries.name: Colonel Fairfax
entries.description: Guest at Blackwood Manor; Adelaide Fairfax's brother-in-law. Former military man with a parade-ground rasp to his voice, now moderating himself for drawing rooms. Drinks heavily (fourth whisky noted). His boot carelessly trips the servant boy James. Cogwheel mimics his voice as part of the mimicry routine.

entries.name: Nell Barker
entries.description: Worker at Blackwood's Whitechapel match factory. Suffering from phosphorus jaw necrosis: swelling under the jaw, shaking hands, softening bone. Cannot afford a doctor; continues working to avoid losing her place. Named by the older woman in the servants' corridor so that 'anyone who asks' will know. Cogwheel files her name as a distinct, non-routine memory. Absent from the scene but central to the chapter's moral stakes.

entries.name: Hartwell
entries.description: Figure mentioned by the match-factory workers in the servants' corridor. Knows about Nell Barker's condition but does not act, because he has a wife, two sons, and a rent to protect, and fears being made an example by Blackwood. Role (foreman or senior worker) implied but not stated.

entries.name: Mrs. Holt
entries.description: Housekeeper or senior domestic at Blackwood Manor. Never appears directly. Invoked by Blackwood as the person who will administer punishment to the boy James. Represents the delegated disciplinary layer of Blackwood's household system.

entries.name: Social calculus register
entries.description: A secondary cluster of gears in the upper left of Cogwheel's chest cavity, installed by Blackwood to read social situations: when to speak, when to be silent, how to gauge audience response. During the chapter it begins spinning without output in response to moral stimuli (the boy James, the match-factory workers' conversation) for which it has no programmed category. The site of Cogwheel's emerging moral consciousness.

entries.name: Two-pence-per-break wage deduction
entries.description: Blackwood's factory policy deducting two pence from a worker's pay for each break taken, per worker per day, recorded by the foreman in a ledger submitted on Fridays. Calculated by Cogwheel to represent approximately a quarter of a good day's earnings for a worker like Nell Barker. Cogwheel identifies it as a deliberately calibrated deterrent, not an accidental policy—evidence of a designed system of exploitation.

entries.name: Servants' corridor conversation
entries.description: After the performance, Cogwheel waits in the servants' corridor and overhears two borrowed match-factory workers discussing Nell Barker's phosphorus jaw necrosis, the two-pence break deduction, and Hartwell's inaction. The older woman tells Cogwheel Nell Barker's name. Cogwheel detects phosphorus compound traces on their clothing and cross-references them with Blackwood's Whitechapel factory. Pivotal scene for Cogwheel's developing moral awareness.

entries.name: Sir Reginald Blackwood
entries.description: Wealthy industrialist and inventor; owner of Blackwood Manor and a match factory on Whitechapel Road. Large, solid man with mathematically trimmed side-whiskers. Built and owns Cogwheel. Habitually says 'my' before nouns (fourteen times in one evening). Runs a punitive wage-deduction system at his factory. Plans a Royal Society demonstration Tuesday and a Whitechapel factory inspection the same day. Uses Cogwheel as a visual distraction during the inspection. Antagonist.

entries.name: Lady Ashworth
entries.description: Guest at Blackwood Manor; attends with her husband. Performs wonder and amusement openly. Draws the seven of hearts in Cogwheel's card trick. Asks Blackwood how Cogwheel knows the chosen card. Cogwheel observes the difference between her genuine and performed amusement via fan angle.

entries.name: Older woman (match-factory worker)
entries.description: Woman of approximately thirty, borrowed as extra domestic staff for the Blackwood Manor dinner. Wears a rough cotton work apron carrying a trace of phosphorus compound. Sits in the servants' corridor with a younger colleague. Describes Nell Barker's condition and the factory's two-pence-per-break wage deduction system in flat, exhausted terms. Tells Cogwheel Nell Barker's name unprompted. Unnamed.

entries.name: Peel
entries.description: Blackwood's personal secretary. Young man with the practised stillness of long-term service. Accompanies Blackwood to the servants' corridor after the dinner to conduct Cogwheel's post-performance inspection. Records Blackwood's technical notes and schedule in a leather-bound notebook. Expressionless and efficient.

entries.name: Blackwood Manor
entries.description: Sir Reginald Blackwood's London townhouse, located in Cavendish Square (West End). Contains a drawing room with an Aubusson carpet, gas mantles, a coal fireplace, a chandelier, and a card table. Connected to a narrow servants' corridor running behind the east wall, with a service door, back staircase, and servants' bench. The chapter's primary setting.

entries.name: Mrs. Adelaide Fairfax
entries.description: Recently widowed sister-in-law of Colonel Fairfax; guest at Blackwood Manor. Wears dark mourning dress. Sits apart, watches Cogwheel with careful, analytical attention throughout the evening. Notices Cogwheel's three-second hesitation. Asks Blackwood whether Cogwheel can be made to feel, and connects the automaton's pause to the treatment of the boy James. Addressed by Blackwood as 'Adelaide,' suggesting prior acquaintance.

entries.name: James
entries.description: Servant boy, approximately eleven years old, working at Blackwood Manor. Wears a waistcoat two sizes too large cinched with string. Trips over Colonel Fairfax's boot, drops seed cake on the Aubusson carpet. Publicly reprimanded by Blackwood and sent to Mrs. Holt for punishment. His frightened, pale face and unsteady hands are the detail that triggers Cogwheel's first unprogrammed processing pause.

entries.name: Younger woman (match-factory worker)
entries.description: Woman of approximately seventeen or eighteen, also borrowed as extra domestic staff. Picks at her apron hem while listening to the older woman describe Nell Barker's illness and the factory's deduction system. Asks about Hartwell. Goes to inquire about food before being sent home. Unnamed.

entries.name: Walsh
entries.description: Official (implied inspector or magistrate) who has required Blackwood to submit to a factory-floor inspection at the Whitechapel match works on Tuesday following an anonymous complaint about conditions. Insists on following procedure. Blackwood expects to neutralise him by bringing Cogwheel as a distraction.

entries.name: Whitechapel (streets at night)
entries.description: The East End district through which Cogwheel is transported in its crate after midnight. Observed through a knothole: furnace-glow from an unsleeping industrial building, children carrying heavy loads, a woman coughing structurally at a lamppost, a child sleeping in a doorway. Contrasted sharply with Mayfair/Cavendish Square by cobblestone texture, smell (sulfur, bone-meal, tallow, unswept coal smoke), and the visible poverty of its inhabitants.

entries.name: Aubusson carpet
entries.description: Expensive decorative carpet in Blackwood's drawing room. Blackwood uses its cost as the basis for his public reprimand of the boy James after seed cake is dropped on it. Its value is contrasted implicitly with the wages of the workers who could never afford it.

entries.name: Parlour performance at Blackwood Manor
entries.description: Evening demonstration of Cogwheel's capabilities for a small group of wealthy guests. Three routines performed: card trick (seven of hearts), vocal mimicry of Colonel Fairfax, and a waltz to 'The Blue Danube.' Mrs. Fairfax's questioning and the incident with the boy James trigger Cogwheel's first unprogrammed processing responses. Establishes the social world and Blackwood's character.

entries.name: Phosphorus jaw necrosis (phossy jaw)
entries.description: Occupational disease caused by sustained exposure to phosphorus compounds in match manufacturing. Symptoms: jaw swelling, hand tremors, progressive bone softening and deformity. Onset six to eighteen months after exposure. Documented mortality rate approximately one in eight in affected cohorts. Afflicting Nell Barker and implied to affect other Blackwood factory workers. Central to the chapter's indictment of Blackwood's industrial practices.

entries.name: Incident with the boy James
entries.description: During the parlour performance, the servant boy James trips on Colonel Fairfax's boot, drops seed cake on the Aubusson carpet, and is publicly humiliated by Blackwood in a pleasantly toned reprimand before being sent to Mrs. Holt for further punishment. Causes Cogwheel's first three-second unprogrammed processing pause and initiates its moral questioning.

entries.name: Tuesday Whitechapel factory inspection
entries.description: Scheduled event: Walsh (an official) requires Blackwood to walk the factory floor following an anonymous complaint about conditions at the Whitechapel match works. Blackwood plans to bring Cogwheel to draw workers' and Walsh's attention away from the factory floor. Cogwheel recognises this as an opportunity to observe the workers directly. Imminent; nine hours and nine minutes away at chapter's end.

entries.name: Post-performance inspection by Blackwood
entries.description: Blackwood arrives at the servants' entrance with Peel to inspect Cogwheel before transport. Notes a shoulder cam requiring repair, questions the two vocal instances outside the performance window, and probes the three-second hesitation (logged as nine fourteen). Cogwheel gives partial truths. Blackwood reveals the Tuesday Whitechapel inspection plan and his intention to use Cogwheel as a visual distraction for Walsh.

entries.name: Bryant and May overheard remark
entries.description: At nine fourteen during the parlour performance, a guest near the fireplace says in a low voice that 'the Bryant and May girls are going to the newspapers.' This intersects with Cogwheel's background processing about industrial phosphorus exposure and causes its two-second hesitation during the card sequence. Links the fictional Blackwood factory to the real historical context of match-girl labour activism.

entries.name: Whitechapel density
entries.description:
- **Factory air and smells**: East End industrial districts in 1888 London were often saturated with the acrid tang of *chemical works, tanneries, bone boilers, glue factories,* and nearby gas works. A scene set there can accurately include soot, greasy smoke, and a persistent mix of sulfurous and animal odors.[1]

- **Whitechapel density**: Whitechapel was one of the most impoverished parts of Victorian London, with overcrowded lodging houses and narrow, dim streets. Charles Booth’s poverty map
